title: GENIE: learned quantum circuits as embedding impurity solvers, and why compactness, not correlation strength, decides when they work

paper.title:
GENIE : learned quantum circuits as embedding impurity solvers, and why
compactness, not correlation strength, decides when they work
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sample-based quantum diagonalization has been combined with density matrix embedding
theory (DMET) to treat molecules larger than a quantum device, but always with
fixed-form circuits, and benchmarked against the embedded exact energy rather than
against classical selection at the same subspace size. We introduce GENIE , a DMET
impurity solver in which a generative transformer learns the sampling circuit and the
quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) energy is the training signal. On
N 2 and hydrogen chains we compare GENIE at equal determinant budget with an oracle,
CIPSI, ASCI and heat-bath CI, and with DMET+SQD using an optimized local unitary cluster
Jastrow circuit. GENIE selects: at 200 determinants (3 % of the space) it is within a
factor of 1.7 of CIPSI at every N 2 geometry and 25–1000 times more accurate than the
determinants a fixed circuit actually samples, while standard SQD reaches good energies by
filling the space, up to 73 % of it for H 14 , still 80–110 kcal mol -1 off, and
under realistic noise its subspace becomes the full space. GENIE does not beat classical
selection: ASCI is 1–5 times better, and on N 2 /cc-pVDZ CIPSI is 12–23 times better
at GENIE ’s uncapped size. GENIE fails where the number of determinants carrying 99 % of
the state approaches the budget, irrespective of the leading-determinant weight, and the
failures are failures of reach, visible in the selected determinants; a deeper circuit
recovers CIPSI quality for H 14 at 2.0 Å. A CCSD/MP2 amplitude count predicts this
number within a factor of three to four over three orders of magnitude, and a router built
on it never recommended GENIE where it then failed, apart from seed-to-seed failures; in a
blind test on water and a twelve-atom hydrogen ring it transferred unchanged. We
also identify two benchmarking pitfalls, the orbital basis of the embedding Hamiltonian
and of the classical baseline, that can manufacture apparent advantages of one to two
orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Sample-based quantum diagonalization uses a quantum computer only to propose determinants: a circuit is prepared and measured, the bitstrings span a subspace, and the Hamiltonian is diagonalized classically in that subspace. In its original form, quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) [ 8 ] , and in its large-scale form with configuration recovery, sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) [ 22 ] , the energy is variational and no expectation value has to be estimated on the device. SQD experiments on up to 77 qubits [ 22 ] and its Krylov variants [ 32 , 20 ] have made the approach the main route to chemistry on present hardware. To treat molecules larger than a device, SQD has been used as the impurity or fragment solver of quantum embedding: density matrix embedding theory (DMET) [ 11 , 12 , 31 ] for hydrogen rings and cyclohexane conformers [ 24 ] and for ligand-like molecules [ 19 ] , the localized active space (LAS) method [ 3 , 4 ] for multi-metal complexes [ 29 ] , and DFT embedding [ 25 ] . All of these sample fixed-form circuits, in practice the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz [ 15 ] , and report the error against the exact (FCI) energy of the embedded problem. The only learned component so far is a classical restricted Boltzmann machine that post-processes the samples [ 18 ] . An energy close to the embedded FCI does not reveal why it is good. It can arise from selection , the circuit sampling the important determinants, or from filling , the subspace becoming a large fraction of the space. Classical selected configuration interaction (SCI), such as CIPSI [ 6 ] , adaptive sampling CI (ASCI) [ 28 ] and heat-bath CI (HCI) [ 5 ] , selects deterministically and is the natural yardstick. Critical assessments found QSCI expansions less compact than classical SCI and sampling inefficient for peaked states [ 21 ] , and a recent review places most claimed QSCI advantages within the classically simulable regime [ 1 ] ; strong classical SCI [ 33 ] raises the bar further, while advantages for sparse ground states have been shown for constructed Hamiltonians [ 10 ] . A different line of work makes the circuit itself learnable. The generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) [ 16 ] trains a transformer to emit sequences of operators from a pool. Trained on the QSCI energy, it produces subspaces up to 50 % smaller than HCI for N 2 in active spaces of up to 32 qubits with 83–98 % fewer two-qubit gates than LUCJ [ 9 ] , and has been scaled to 40 qubits [ 2 ] . These studies work in a complete active space, without embedding, and compare against HCI only. Here we combine the two lines and ask a sharper question than “is the energy good”: does the circuit select, how does it compare with the best classical heuristics at the same number of determinants, and can one tell beforehand whether it will work? Our contributions are: (i) GENIE , a DMET impurity solver whose sampling circuit is learned by GQE, with the embedding Hamiltonian expressed in the embedded mean-field basis so that operator pool, reference determinant and Hamiltonian are consistent (Sec. II ); (ii) an equal-budget protocol that compares every GENIE run at its final subspace size N N with an oracle, CIPSI, ASCI and HCI in two orbital bases, and with DMET+SQD restricted to the determinants actually sampled (Secs. III.1 – III.3 ); (iii) the finding that failures are governed by the compactness of the impurity wavefunction relative to the budget rather than by correlation strength (Sec. III.5 ); and (iv) an amplitude-based estimate and router that predict these failures in advance, validated in a blind test on new systems (Secs. III.6 and III.7 ). Section III.8 discusses the scope of an impurity-level study and the LAS alternative, and Sec. III.9 resources and hardware feasibility; the appendices contain every data table behind the figures.

sections.heading: II.1 Density matrix embedding
sections.text: The whole molecule is treated at the unrestricted Hartree–Fock (UHF) level. The impurity orbitals are the active orbitals chosen with atomic valence active space (AVAS) projection [ 23 ] onto atom-resolved labels (e.g. the 1s functions of the central atoms of a hydrogen chain). A Schmidt decomposition of the reference one-particle density matrix gives a bath of at most the same size; impurity plus bath span the embedding space of n n orbitals, in which the interacting Hamiltonian is H emb = \displaystyle H_{\mathrm{emb}}={} E core + ∑ p ​ q ​ σ h p ​ q ​ a p ​ σ † ​ a q ​ σ \displaystyle E_{\mathrm{core}}+\sum_{pq\sigma}h_{pq}\,a^{\dagger}_{p\sigma}a_{q\sigma} + 1 2 ∑ p ​ q ​ r ​ s ​ σ ​ τ ( p q | r s ) a p ​ σ † a r ​ τ † a s ​ τ a q ​ σ , \displaystyle+\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{pqrs\sigma\tau}(pq|rs)\,a^{\dagger}_{p\sigma}a^{\dagger}_{r\tau}a_{s\tau}a_{q\sigma}, (1) with the frozen environment folded into E core E_{\mathrm{core}} and h p ​ q h_{pq} [ 11 , 12 , 31 ] . Unlike the textbook mean-field bath, the Schmidt decomposition acts on a correlated reference density, a CASCI in the AVAS space, and the bath size is chosen adaptively from the singular-value spectrum; the scheme is one-shot, without a correlation potential (App. A ). An embedded RHF is solved in the embedding space with E core E_{\mathrm{core}} as constant.

sections.heading: Orbital basis.
sections.text: Equation ( 1 ) is naturally expressed in the raw (Schmidt) basis. We rotate it into the embedded RHF molecular-orbital (MO) basis, h → C 𝖳 ​ h ​ C h\to C^{\mathsf{T}}hC and likewise for ( p ​ q | r ​ s ) (pq|rs) . Energies are invariant, but this step is essential for a learned circuit: the circuit starts from “the lowest orbitals occupied” and its excitation operators are indexed by occupied and virtual MOs. In the raw basis the starting determinant lies 20 000–40 000 kcal mol -1 above RHF and GENIE errors were 40–95 kcal mol -1 ; after rotation they fall by up to five orders of magnitude (App. B , Table 5 ). A complete-active-space GQE pipeline is unaffected, because its basis already is the MO basis, which is why the problem is easy to miss when such a pipeline is moved into an embedding.

sections.heading: II.2 Quantum-selected configuration interaction
sections.text: A state | ψ ⟩ |\psi\rangle prepared on 2 ​ n 2n qubits (Jordan–Wigner) is measured N s N_{s} times. After discarding bitstrings with the wrong electron numbers and completing the set under α ↔ β \alpha\leftrightarrow\beta exchange (spin completion), the distinct determinants form 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , | 𝒮 | ≤ N |\mathcal{S}|\leq N , where N N is the budget (cap). The QSCI energy is the lowest eigenvalue of the projected Hamiltonian, E 𝒮 = min ⁡ eig ⁡ [ ⟨ D I | H emb | D J ⟩ ] I , J ∈ 𝒮 , E_{\mathcal{S}}=\min\operatorname{eig}\,\bigl[\langle D_{I}|H_{\mathrm{emb}}|D_{J}\rangle\bigr]_{I,J\in\mathcal{S}}, (2) which is variational, E 𝒮 ≥ E FCI emb E_{\mathcal{S}}\geq E_{\mathrm{FCI}}^{\mathrm{emb}} . SQD [ 22 ] instead diagonalizes in the Cartesian product of all sampled α \alpha strings with all sampled β \beta strings (“product” subspace) and recovers configurations broken by noise; we also evaluate the “list” subspace of the sampled ( α , β ) (\alpha,\beta) pairs only, which isolates what the circuit selects.

(a) Classical embedding: an AVAS impurity and its Schmidt bath define the embedding Hamiltonian H emb H_{\mathrm{emb}} of n n orbitals ( 2 ​ n 2n qubits); the embedded RHF provides CCSD amplitudes (operator angles and compactness estimate) and the orbitals into which H emb H_{\mathrm{emb}} is rotated, so that operator pool, reference determinant and Hamiltonian share one basis. sections.heading: Refinement.
sections.text: As in Ref. [ 9 ] , the QSCI solutions of the circuits of one epoch are merged into one sparse wavefunction (local refinement), which is then merged with the result of all previous epochs (global refinement). Each merge solves the generalized eigenvalue problem in the non-orthogonal basis of the input wavefunctions and keeps the N N determinants with the largest weights. Refinement is purely classical and generates no new determinants: the final set 𝒮 ∗ \mathcal{S}^{\ast} consists of determinants sampled by some circuit during training. It is therefore the product of all circuits executed in training, not of a single circuit, for H 14 at 2.0 Å the best single circuit samples 1 400–3 400 distinct determinants, the refined set holds 10 4 10^{4} , and the quantum cost of a GENIE point is that of the whole training run (Sec. III.9 ). Unless stated, n g = 80 n_{g}=80 , 120 epochs, 100 circuits per epoch (12 000 circuits per run, N s = 10 5 N_{\mathrm{s}}=10^{5} shots each, i.e. 1.2 × 10 9 1.2\times 10^{9} shots), a QSCI cap of N = 10 4 N=10^{4} (or budgets of 100 and 200), and three seeds (App. J , Table 16 ); runs that stop before 120 epochs are rejected by the pipeline. All simulations are noiseless state-vector simulations with CUDA-Q [ 17 ] . Because QSCI energies are variational, the best of k k seeds is a valid result at k k -fold cost.

sections.heading: II.4 Equal-budget protocol and baselines
sections.text: For every finished GENIE run with final subspace size N N we evaluate, on the same H emb H_{\mathrm{emb}} and at the same N N , the variational energies of (a) an oracle , the N N determinants with largest | c I | |c_{I}| in the exact embedded ground state, re-diagonalized (a reference, not a method); (b) CIPSI [ 6 ] , grown by Epstein–Nesbet second-order contributions until exactly N N determinants; (c) ASCI [ 28 ] , fixed-size and seeded with CIPSI, which can drop determinants; and (d) a fixed-size HCI [ 5 ] (App. C ). Selection is basis dependent, so each selector is run in both the raw and the MO basis and the better value is the reference. Errors are quoted against the embedding FCI. For DMET+SQD we use the same embedding and an LUCJ circuit [ 15 ] with all-pairs interactions and two repetitions, CCSD-initialized and optimized with the linear method of ffsim [ 27 ] , 10 4 10^{4} or 10 5 10^{5} shots, and six configuration-recovery iterations [ 22 ] (Qiskit addon [ 7 ] ). Noise is modeled on the FakeSherbrooke backend (App. E ).

sections.heading: III Numerical results
sections.text: We study N 2 /STO-3G at R = 1.1 R=1.1 – 2.5 2.5 Å, where the AVAS N 2s2p impurity plus bath spans the full valence space (9–10 orbitals, 18–20 qubits), so that the embedding error vanishes and the solver is isolated; N 2 /cc-pVDZ (13 of 28 orbitals, 26 qubits, 2.9 × 10 6 2.9\times 10^{6} determinants); linear H 10 and H 14 /STO-3G with central-atom impurities at R = 1.0 R=1.0 , 1.5 and 2.0 Å (up to 20 qubits, 63 504 determinants); and [Fe(H 2 O) 4 ] 2 bpym 4+ for the LAS route [ 29 , 4 ] . All systems and embeddings are listed in Table 4 . Software: PySCF [ 26 ] , CUDA-Q [ 17 ] , Qiskit [ 7 ] , ffsim [ 27 ] and our package QuEnAIS [ 14 ] .

sections.heading: III.1 Selection at equal budget
sections.text: Figure 2: N 2 /STO-3G, error against the embedding FCI at fixed budgets of (a) 100 and (b) 200 determinants: GENIE (CCSD angles, 80 operators, three seeds), CIPSI and ASCI (MO basis), and the oracle (dashed). Dotted line: 1 kcal mol -1 . Full data in Table 6 . Figure 2 shows the central comparison. At 200 determinants (about 3 % of the space) GENIE is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI at every geometry [Fig. 2 (b)], including 2.5 Å where the leading determinant carries only 10 % of the weight. ASCI is 1–5 times better than both and coincides with the oracle: GENIE reaches CIPSI but not ASCI quality. One 200-determinant seed in three fails (17 kcal mol -1 at 2.5 Å). At 100 determinants GENIE fails at 1.8–2.5 Å [Fig. 2 (a)], with errors of 17–50 kcal mol -1 against 0.5–2 kcal mol -1 for CIPSI; only one seed at 2.1 Å succeeds. Without a cap, GENIE keeps 600–1 100 determinants and reaches 10 − 2 10^{-2} – 10 − 4 10^{-4} kcal mol -1 ; with free angles it reaches the embedding FCI using 25–51 % of the space.

sections.heading: III.2 Two benchmarking pitfalls, and seed variance
sections.text: Figure 3: (a) GENIE error for N 2 /STO-3G with the embedding Hamiltonian in the raw Schmidt basis and in the embedded MO basis (no cap, CCSD angles, 80 operators; Table 5 ). (b) Classical selectors at N = 200 N=200 , selected in the raw basis (open) and in the MO basis (filled); same Hamiltonian, energies are basis invariant, only the selection changes. (c) Five GENIE seeds in a plain CAS(10e,8o) N 2 problem at 2.1 Å, N = 200 N=200 , against CIPSI and the oracle. Three effects can make a quantum selection scheme look much better or worse than it is (Fig. 3 ). First, the basis of the Hamiltonian: in the raw Schmidt basis the learned circuit starts from a determinant tens of thousands of kcal mol -1 above RHF and fails by 46–95 kcal mol -1 ; in the MO basis the same pipeline reaches 10 − 2 10^{-2} – 10 − 4 10^{-4} kcal mol -1 [Fig. 3 (a)]. Second, the basis of the baseline : CIPSI selected in the raw basis is 2–36 times worse than in the MO basis, HCI and ASCI behave alike [Fig. 3 (b)]. Against raw-basis CIPSI, GENIE appeared 6–38 times better, an advantage that disappears under a fair baseline. Our fixed-size HCI is moreover 3–65 times worse than CIPSI on the same problems (Table 6 ). This fixed-size variant is weaker than production semistochastic HCI, which we did not run; the point is that HCI’s quality depends on its implementation and size control, so advantages measured against HCI alone [ 9 , 30 ] should be read with care. Third, seed variance is large [Fig. 3 (c)]: five seeds span a factor of 300; the best run beats CIPSI by 10 × 10\times , the median is 3 × 3\times worse and one in five fails (App. C ). A single favorable run is therefore not evidence of an advantage; we report all seeds, and since QSCI energies are variational, the best of k k seeds is a legitimate result at k k -fold cost.

sections.heading: III.3 Selection versus filling
sections.text: Figure 4: N 2 /STO-3G at (a) 1.8 and (b) 2.5 Å: error versus subspace size for the determinants actually sampled by DMET+SQD (“list” subspace, optimized LUCJ, 10 4 10^{4} and 10 5 10^{5} shots), GENIE (budgets 100 and 200) and CIPSI. Full data in Table 8 . Restricted to the determinants it samples, DMET+SQD is 1.4–100 times less accurate than CIPSI at equal size (Table 8 ), and more shots do not help at 2.5 Å: 37.4 and 36.4 kcal mol -1 for 139 and 309 determinants. The optimized fixed-form circuit does not reach the important determinants of a stretched bond. With fewer determinants GENIE is 25–50 times (1.8 Å) and 500–1000 times (2.5 Å) more accurate (Fig. 4 ), i.e. it behaves like CIPSI rather than like the sampler. Figure 5: (a) N 2 /STO-3G, DMET+SQD with optimized LUCJ: range over three seeds of the product-subspace energy (bars), the sampled-list energy (diamonds, mean and range) and CIPSI at the size of the list (squares). (b) N 2 /cc-pVDZ (26 qubits): error versus subspace fraction for DMET+SQD (unoptimized LUCJ, 10 4 10^{4} / 10 5 10^{5} shots), CIPSI (raw basis) at the same sizes, GENIE (budget 200 and uncapped), and the best of CIPSI and ASCI in the MO basis at GENIE ’s sizes; filled 1.1 Å, open 2.1 Å. The good energies usually reported for SQD come from the product subspace. In small embeddings the α × β \alpha\times\beta product of the sampled strings covers most of the space; adding random exploration shots made every tested system exact, including N 2 /cc-pVDZ, by covering 99.9–100 % of spaces of up to 2.9 × 10 6 2.9\times 10^{6} determinants (App. D ). This is exact diagonalization, not compression. Per seed, the product energy scatters over up to two orders of magnitude while the list energy is stable and far from CIPSI [Fig. 5 (a)]. Noise makes this explicit (App. E , Table 10 ). Under a FakeSherbrooke noise model (N 2 , 1.1 Å; routed LUCJ with 3 499 CX gates, estimated circuit fidelity 0.05 at one tenth of present-day error rates and 10 − 13 10^{-13} at present-day rates), the product subspace becomes the full space and its energy exact. The sampled list improves with noise: from 5.5–6.7 kcal mol -1 with 87–95 determinants without noise to 0.05–0.20 kcal mol -1 with 5 600 determinants (39 % of the space) at one tenth of present-day rates, and 0.2–2.0 kcal mol -1 with 7 600 (53 %) at present-day rates. Better energies from a noisier device are the signature of filling: noise spreads the samples over the space, and the classical diagonalization does the rest. On N 2 /cc-pVDZ (26 qubits, 2.9 × 10 6 2.9\times 10^{6} and 8.5 × 10 5 8.5\times 10^{5} determinants at 1.1 and 2.1 Å), GENIE is again far ahead of DMET+SQD at similar size, 6.2 against 29 kcal mol -1 and 22.5 against 94 kcal mol -1 at about 200 determinants, and without cap reaches 0.48 and 0.62 kcal mol -1 with 0.3 and 1.2 % of the space [Fig. 5 (b), Table 9 ]. Against classical selection in the MO basis at the same sizes it is behind, however: tied with CIPSI and ASCI at 200 determinants and 1.1 Å (6.25 vs. 6.14), 1.9 times behind at 2.1 Å (22.5 vs. 11.7), and 23 and 12 times behind uncapped (0.48 vs. 0.021 and 0.62 vs. 0.053 kcal mol -1 ). In the larger space, the 80-operator circuit reaches chemical accuracy but not the compact expansion that CIPSI finds.

For H 14 , DMET truncates the system to 9–10 of 14 orbitals and the embedding is genuine (Table 1 , Fig. 6 ). Near equilibrium GENIE ties with CIPSI at 200 determinants, and with N ≈ 7 000 N\approx 7\,000 free-angle circuits reach the embedding FCI. At 1.5 Å it is 1.2 times behind CIPSI at 10 4 10^{4} determinants. At 2.0 Å and 80 operators it fails: 68–70 kcal mol -1 against 6–7 kcal mol -1 for CIPSI and ASCI at the same 10 4 10^{4} determinants, identically for both seeds and both angle schemes. At 1.5 and 2.0 Å every 80-operator run fills the cap of 10 4 10^{4} determinants (15.7 % of the space), so the limit is not the number of determinants but which ones the circuit reaches. Doubling the circuit to 160 operators recovers CIPSI quality [Fig. 6 (b)]: 7.92 kcal mol -1 against 7.00 for CIPSI; 320 operators add nothing (8.09 kcal mol -1 ). At 1.5 Å, where the 80-operator circuit already reaches the important determinants, 160 operators change nothing (3.03 against 3.04–3.19 kcal mol -1 ): depth helps only where reach is the limit. The training curves (Fig. 7 ) show how. With 80 operators the best energy stops improving after a few epochs. With 160 and 320 operators it drops in steps, as the transformer finds sequences that reach new groups of determinants, and settles after 50–70 epochs. Refinement matters: the raw circuit’s subspace gives 14.6 kcal mol -1 at 160 operators, the refined set 7.9 kcal mol -1 . For N 2 at 2.5 Å the same curves show the seed failures of Sec. III.2 : two of three seeds at N = 200 N=200 jump to below 0.1 kcal mol -1 within 25–45 epochs, the third never does [Fig. 7 (b)]. sections.heading: III.8 Scope and the LAS alternative
sections.text: This is an impurity-level study: every error above is measured against the exact solution of the same embedding Hamiltonian, which isolates the solver. The total DMET energy of a single impurity is not a whole-molecule energy; for H 10 it lies 77–386 kcal mol -1 above whole-molecule FCI, increasingly so on stretching, independently of the solver (App. H ). A whole-molecule comparison requires all fragments and an energy partitioning, which we leave to future work, as do the embedding errors that impurity-level benchmarks cannot see [ 24 , 19 ] . For spread states the router points to fragment methods. On H 10 , where whole-molecule FCI is available, LASSQD agrees with LASSCF to within 1 kcal mol -1 , but the error against FCI depends on the fragmentation: 38.5, 41.0 and 19.5 kcal mol -1 with H 2 -unit fragments at 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 Å, and 84.5, 32.5 and 9.5 kcal mol -1 with two halves (App. H ). For [Fe(H 2 O) 4 ] 2 bpym 4+ , where a DMET impurity would need about 40 qubits, LAS needs two ten-qubit fragments; our LASSCF lies 1.05 m E h E_{\mathrm{h}} below the published value [ 29 ] , and LASSQD warm-started from it reproduces it to 0.3 ​ μ ​ E h 0.3\,\mu E_{\mathrm{h}} for all four circuit/seed combinations (App. I ).

Against classical selection it buys nothing in these systems; the comparison with CIPSI is lost by two to three orders of magnitude in time. The circuits are not executable on present hardware. With an effective error p p per CX the circuit fidelity is roughly e − p ​ n CX e^{-p\,n_{\mathrm{CX}}} . At the error rates of our noise model ( p ≈ 8.5 × 10 − 3 p\approx 8.5\times 10^{-3} , which reproduces the estimated fidelity 1.4 × 10 − 13 1.4\times 10^{-13} of the routed 3 499-CX LUCJ circuit), the 80-operator N 2 circuits (7 400 CX) have a fidelity of 10 − 27 10^{-27} and the H 14 circuits below 10 − 39 10^{-39} . Shorter circuits are the obvious lever: gate-penalized rewards and gate-efficient pools reduced two-qubit counts by 83–98 % in Ref. [ 9 ] .

sections.heading: IV Conclusion and discussion
sections.text: Within DMET, GENIE is, to our knowledge, the first quantum impurity solver whose sampling circuit is learned. Measured at equal subspace size against classical selection rather than against the embedded FCI, it closes the gap of one to three orders of magnitude between fixed-form sampling and classical selection. It reaches CIPSI quality at small budgets but not ASCI quality, and in a 26-qubit embedding it stays an order of magnitude behind CIPSI at its own uncapped size, at two to three orders of magnitude more wall-clock time and with circuits of 10 4 10^{4} CX gates that require fault-tolerant hardware. Standard DMET+SQD reaches good energies by filling the space, which noise makes complete; where filling is not possible, as for H 14 , it fails by 75–130 kcal mol -1 . Both observations are consistent with critical assessments of QSCI [ 21 , 1 ] and with the strength of modern classical SCI [ 33 ] . The compactness criterion held in a blind test on two new systems, where it predicted the failure for the stretched hydrogen ring and success for water. It is not specific to GENIE . It applies to any quantum selection scheme, including Krylov variants [ 32 , 20 ] and DMET with learned classical post-processing [ 18 ] : a sampler can pay off only where the state is compact in some representation and yet hard to find classically, a regime none of our systems reaches, and the one in which claimed advantages have so far been shown [ 10 ] . For spread states, localized orbitals, in which stretched H 14 is 1.3–1.8 times more compact, paired or generalized excitation pools and multireference initial states are the natural next steps; on noisy hardware, configuration recovery [ 22 ] becomes relevant to GENIE as well. Methodologically we recommend that quantum subspace methods report the subspace size and compare against CIPSI and ASCI at that size, in the orbital basis in which those methods perform best; that seed statistics be reported; and that embedding studies separate the solver error, as here, from the embedding error against whole-molecule references. A cheap compactness estimate should accompany any claim of where a method is expected to work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Systems and DMET implementation
sections.text: The impurity is selected with AVAS [ 23 ] on atom-indexed labels. The impurity orbitals and their Schmidt bath, obtained from the reference one-particle density matrix, span the embedding space. In detail: (i) Mean field. The whole molecule is described by UHF. For N 2 , H 10 , H 14 , H 2 O and the H 12 ring at 2.0 Å it coincides with RHF to < 10 − 5 <10^{-5} kcal mol -1 . For the H 12 ring at 1.0 and 1.5 Å it breaks spin symmetry and lies 53.5 and 5.2 kcal mol -1 below RHF, as expected for a 4 ​ n 4n ring with a near-degenerate frontier pair. Only the environment and E core E_{\mathrm{core}} depend on this choice; all solver errors are measured against the exact solution of the same embedding Hamiltonian, and the embedded reference for the circuits is the closed-shell embedded RHF. (ii) Impurity. The impurity orbitals are the AVAS active orbitals (molecular orbitals of mixed atomic character, not localized atomic orbitals). (iii) Reference density. Instead of the mean-field density, the Schmidt decomposition acts on a CASCI density in the AVAS space, with the active one-electron Hamiltonian screened by the mean-field potential of the non-active electrons, combined with the mean-field density outside the active space. This places the bath where the correlated density couples impurity and environment. (iv) Bath. The impurity–environment block of the reference density (Löwdin basis) is decomposed by singular value decomposition; singular values below 10 − 8 10^{-8} are discarded, so a bath of zero orbitals is allowed. The number of bath orbitals is the larger of the position of the largest gap in the singular values and the number needed to cover 99.9 % of ∑ σ 2 \sum\sigma^{2} , capped at the number of impurity orbitals and at 18 embedding orbitals in total. (v) Electron count. The number of embedded electrons is the rounded trace of the reference density in the embedding space, not the active-space count. (vi) Environment. The environment density is the reference density projected onto the complement of the embedding space; it enters h p ​ q h_{pq} through Coulomb and exchange terms. E core E_{\mathrm{core}} is fixed so that the projected UHF density reproduces the whole-molecule UHF energy within the embedding Hamiltonian. (vii) Chemical potential. A one-shot grand-canonical shift h → h − μ ​ 𝟙 h\to h-\mu\mathbb{1} , E core → E core + μ ​ N E_{\mathrm{core}}\to E_{\mathrm{core}}+\mu N is applied; it cancels exactly for the fixed-particle-number solvers used here. (viii) One-shot. No correlation potential is fitted and no self-consistency loop is run; the energy reported is that of the embedding Hamiltonian (Sec. III.8 ). Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.41957v1 [quant-ph] 30 Oct 2026 GENIE : learned quantum circuits as embedding impurity solvers, and why compactness, not correlation strength, decides when they work Awadhoot Vijay Loharkar Email: awadhoot.vijay.loharkar@itwm.fraunhofer.de Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Industrial Mathematics ITWM, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany Arcesio Castañeda Medina Email: arcesio.castaneda.medina@itwm.fraunhofer.de Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Industrial Mathematics ITWM, 67663 Kaiserslautern, Germany October 30, 2026 Abstract Sample-based quantum diagonalization has been combined with density matrix embedding theory (DMET) to treat molecules larger than a quantum device, but always with fixed-form circuits, and benchmarked against the embedded exact energy rather than against classical selection at the same subspace size. We introduce GENIE , a DMET impurity solver in which a generative transformer learns the sampling circuit and the quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) energy is the training signal. On N 2 and hydrogen chains we compare GENIE at equal determinant budget with an oracle, CIPSI, ASCI and heat-bath CI, and with DMET+SQD using an optimized local unitary cluster Jastrow circuit. GENIE selects: at 200 determinants (3 % of the space) it is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI at every N 2 geometry and 25–1000 times more accurate than the determinants a fixed circuit actually samples, while standard SQD reaches good energies by filling the space, up to 73 % of it for H 14 , still 80–110 kcal mol -1 off, and under realistic noise its subspace becomes the full space. GENIE does not beat classical selection: ASCI is 1–5 times better, and on N 2 /cc-pVDZ CIPSI is 12–23 times better at GENIE ’s uncapped size. GENIE fails where the number of determinants carrying 99 % of the state approaches the budget, irrespective of the leading-determinant weight, and the failures are failures of reach, visible in the selected determinants; a deeper circuit recovers CIPSI quality for H 14 at 2.0 Å. A CCSD/MP2 amplitude count predicts this number within a factor of three to four over three orders of magnitude, and a router built on it never recommended GENIE where it then failed, apart from seed-to-seed failures; in a blind test on water and a twelve-atom hydrogen ring it transferred unchanged. We also identify two benchmarking pitfalls, the orbital basis of the embedding Hamiltonian and of the classical baseline, that can manufacture apparent advantages of one to two orders of magnitude. I Introduction Sample-based quantum diagonalization uses a quantum computer only to propose determinants: a circuit is prepared and measured, the bitstrings span a subspace, and the Hamiltonian is diagonalized classically in that subspace. In its original form, quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) [ 8 ] , and in its large-scale form with configuration recovery, sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) [ 22 ] , the energy is variational and no expectation value has to be estimated on the device. SQD experiments on up to 77 qubits [ 22 ] and its Krylov variants [ 32 , 20 ] have made the approach the main route to chemistry on present hardware. To treat molecules larger than a device, SQD has been used as the impurity or fragment solver of quantum embedding: density matrix embedding theory (DMET) [ 11 , 12 , 31 ] for hydrogen rings and cyclohexane conformers [ 24 ] and for ligand-like molecules [ 19 ] , the localized active space (LAS) method [ 3 , 4 ] for multi-metal complexes [ 29 ] , and DFT embedding [ 25 ] . All of these sample fixed-form circuits, in practice the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz [ 15 ] , and report the error against the exact (FCI) energy of the embedded problem. The only learned component so far is a classical restricted Boltzmann machine that post-processes the samples [ 18 ] . An energy close to the embedded FCI does not reveal why it is good. It can arise from selection , the circuit sampling the important determinants, or from filling , the subspace becoming a large fraction of the space. Classical selected configuration interaction (SCI), such as CIPSI [ 6 ] , adaptive sampling CI (ASCI) [ 28 ] and heat-bath CI (HCI) [ 5 ] , selects deterministically and is the natural yardstick. Critical assessments found QSCI expansions less compact than classical SCI and sampling inefficient for peaked states [ 21 ] , and a recent review places most claimed QSCI advantages within the classically simulable regime [ 1 ] ; strong classical SCI [ 33 ] raises the bar further, while advantages for sparse ground states have been shown for constructed Hamiltonians [ 10 ] . A different line of work makes the circuit itself learnable. The generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) [ 16 ] trains a transformer to emit sequences of operators from a pool. Trained on the QSCI energy, it produces subspaces up to 50 % smaller than HCI for N 2 in active spaces of up to 32 qubits with 83–98 % fewer two-qubit gates than LUCJ [ 9 ] , and has been scaled to 40 qubits [ 2 ] . These studies work in a complete active space, without embedding, and compare against HCI only. Here we combine the two lines and ask a sharper question than “is the energy good”: does the circuit select, how does it compare with the best classical heuristics at the same number of determinants, and can one tell beforehand whether it will work? Our contributions are: (i) GENIE , a DMET impurity solver whose sampling circuit is learned by GQE, with the embedding Hamiltonian expressed in the embedded mean-field basis so that operator pool, reference determinant and Hamiltonian are consistent (Sec. II ); (ii) an equal-budget protocol that compares every GENIE run at its final subspace size N N with an oracle, CIPSI, ASCI and HCI in two orbital bases, and with DMET+SQD restricted to the determinants actually sampled (Secs. III.1 – III.3 ); (iii) the finding that failures are governed by the compactness of the impurity wavefunction relative to the budget rather than by correlation strength (Sec. III.5 ); and (iv) an amplitude-based estimate and router that predict these failures in advance, validated in a blind test on new systems (Secs. III.6 and III.7 ). Section III.8 discusses the scope of an impurity-level study and the LAS alternative, and Sec. III.9 resources and hardware feasibility; the appendices contain every data table behind the figures. II Methods II.1 Density matrix embedding The whole molecule is treated at the unrestricted Hartree–Fock (UHF) level. The impurity orbitals are the active orbitals chosen with atomic valence active space (AVAS) projection [ 23 ] onto atom-resolved labels (e.g. the 1s functions of the central atoms of a hydrogen chain). Unlike the textbook mean-field bath, the Schmidt decomposition acts on a correlated reference density, a CASCI in the AVAS space, and the bath size is chosen adaptively from the singular-value spectrum; the scheme is one-shot, without a correlation potential (App. A ). An embedded RHF is solved in the embedding space with E core E_{\mathrm{core}} as constant. Orbital basis. Equation ( 1 ) is naturally expressed in the raw (Schmidt) basis. We rotate it into the embedded RHF molecular-orbital (MO) basis, h → C 𝖳 ​ h ​ C h\to C^{\mathsf{T}}hC and likewise for ( p ​ q | r ​ s ) (pq|rs) . Energies are invariant, but this step is essential for a learned circuit: the circuit starts from “the lowest orbitals occupied” and its excitation operators are indexed by occupied and virtual MOs. In the raw basis the starting determinant lies 20 000–40 000 kcal mol -1 above RHF and GENIE errors were 40–95 kcal mol -1 ; after rotation they fall by up to five orders of magnitude (App. B , Table 5 ). A complete-active-space GQE pipeline is unaffected, because its basis already is the MO basis, which is why the problem is easy to miss when such a pipeline is moved into an embedding. II.4 Equal-budget protocol and baselines For every finished GENIE run with final subspace size N N we evaluate, on the same H emb H_{\mathrm{emb}} and at the same N N , the variational energies of (a) an oracle , the N N determinants with largest | c I | |c_{I}| in the exact embedded ground state, re-diagonalized (a reference, not a method); (b) CIPSI [ 6 ] , grown by Epstein–Nesbet second-order contributions until exactly N N determinants; (c) ASCI [ 28 ] , fixed-size and seeded with CIPSI, which can drop determinants; and (d) a fixed-size HCI [ 5 ] (App. C ). Selection is basis dependent, so each selector is run in both the raw and the MO basis and the better value is the reference. Errors are quoted against the embedding FCI. III.1 Selection at equal budget Figure 2: N 2 /STO-3G, error against the embedding FCI at fixed budgets of (a) 100 and (b) 200 determinants: GENIE (CCSD angles, 80 operators, three seeds), CIPSI and ASCI (MO basis), and the oracle (dashed). Dotted line: 1 kcal mol -1 . Full data in Table 6 . Figure 2 shows the central comparison. At 200 determinants (about 3 % of the space) GENIE is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI at every geometry [Fig. 2 (b)], including 2.5 Å where the leading determinant carries only 10 % of the weight. ASCI is 1–5 times better than both and coincides with the oracle: GENIE reaches CIPSI but not ASCI quality. One 200-determinant seed in three fails (17 kcal mol -1 at 2.5 Å). At 100 determinants GENIE fails at 1.8–2.5 Å [Fig. 2 (a)], with errors of 17–50 kcal mol -1 against 0.5–2 kcal mol -1 for CIPSI; only one seed at 2.1 Å succeeds. Without a cap, GENIE keeps 600–1 100 determinants and reaches 10 − 2 10^{-2} – 10 − 4 10^{-4} kcal mol -1 ; with free angles it reaches the embedding FCI using 25–51 % of the space. III.2 Two benchmarking pitfalls, and seed variance Figure 3: (a) GENIE error for N 2 /STO-3G with the embedding Hamiltonian in the raw Schmidt basis and in the embedded MO basis (no cap, CCSD angles, 80 operators; Table 5 ). (b) Classical selectors at N = 200 N=200 , selected in the raw basis (open) and in the MO basis (filled); same Hamiltonian, energies are basis invariant, only the selection changes. (c) Five GENIE seeds in a plain CAS(10e,8o) N 2 problem at 2.1 Å, N = 200 N=200 , against CIPSI and the oracle. Three effects can make a quantum selection scheme look much better or worse than it is (Fig. 3 ). First, the basis of the Hamiltonian: in the raw Schmidt basis the learned circuit starts from a determinant tens of thousands of kcal mol -1 above RHF and fails by 46–95 kcal mol -1 ; in the MO basis the same pipeline reaches 10 − 2 10^{-2} – 10 − 4 10^{-4} kcal mol -1 [Fig. 3 (a)]. Second, the basis of the baseline : CIPSI selected in the raw basis is 2–36 times worse than in the MO basis, HCI and ASCI behave alike [Fig. 3 (b)]. Against raw-basis CIPSI, GENIE appeared 6–38 times better, an advantage that disappears under a fair baseline. Our fixed-size HCI is moreover 3–65 times worse than CIPSI on the same problems (Table 6 ). This fixed-size variant is weaker than production semistochastic HCI, which we did not run; the point is that HCI’s quality depends on its implementation and size control, so advantages measured against HCI alone [ 9 , 30 ] should be read with care. Third, seed variance is large [Fig. 3 (c)]: five seeds span a factor of 300; the best run beats CIPSI by 10 × 10\times , the median is 3 × 3\times worse and one in five fails (App. C ). A single favorable run is therefore not evidence of an advantage; we report all seeds, and since QSCI energies are variational, the best of k k seeds is a legitimate result at k k -fold cost. III.3 Selection versus filling Figure 4: N 2 /STO-3G at (a) 1.8 and (b) 2.5 Å: error versus subspace size for the determinants actually sampled by DMET+SQD (“list” subspace, optimized LUCJ, 10 4 10^{4} and 10 5 10^{5} shots), GENIE (budgets 100 and 200) and CIPSI. Full data in Table 8 . Restricted to the determinants it samples, DMET+SQD is 1.4–100 times less accurate than CIPSI at equal size (Table 8 ), and more shots do not help at 2.5 Å: 37.4 and 36.4 kcal mol -1 for 139 and 309 determinants. The optimized fixed-form circuit does not reach the important determinants of a stretched bond. With fewer determinants GENIE is 25–50 times (1.8 Å) and 500–1000 times (2.5 Å) more accurate (Fig. 4 ), i.e. it behaves like CIPSI rather than like the sampler. Figure 5: (a) N 2 /STO-3G, DMET+SQD with optimized LUCJ: range over three seeds of the product-subspace energy (bars), the sampled-list energy (diamonds, mean and range) and CIPSI at the size of the list (squares). (b) N 2 /cc-pVDZ (26 qubits): error versus subspace fraction for DMET+SQD (unoptimized LUCJ, 10 4 10^{4} / 10 5 10^{5} shots), CIPSI (raw basis) at the same sizes, GENIE (budget 200 and uncapped), and the best of CIPSI and ASCI in the MO basis at GENIE ’s sizes; filled 1.1 Å, open 2.1 Å. The good energies usually reported for SQD come from the product subspace. In small embeddings the α × β \alpha\times\beta product of the sampled strings covers most of the space; adding random exploration shots made every tested system exact, including N 2 /cc-pVDZ, by covering 99.9–100 % of spaces of up to 2.9 × 10 6 2.9\times 10^{6} determinants (App. D ). This is exact diagonalization, not compression. Per seed, the product energy scatters over up to two orders of magnitude while the list energy is stable and far from CIPSI [Fig. 5 (a)]. Noise makes this explicit (App. E , Table 10 ). Under a FakeSherbrooke noise model (N 2 , 1.1 Å; routed LUCJ with 3 499 CX gates, estimated circuit fidelity 0.05 at one tenth of present-day error rates and 10 − 13 10^{-13} at present-day rates), the product subspace becomes the full space and its energy exact. The sampled list improves with noise: from 5.5–6.7 kcal mol -1 with 87–95 determinants without noise to 0.05–0.20 kcal mol -1 with 5 600 determinants (39 % of the space) at one tenth of present-day rates, and 0.2–2.0 kcal mol -1 with 7 600 (53 %) at present-day rates. Better energies from a noisier device are the signature of filling: noise spreads the samples over the space, and the classical diagonalization does the rest. On N 2 /cc-pVDZ (26 qubits, 2.9 × 10 6 2.9\times 10^{6} and 8.5 × 10 5 8.5\times 10^{5} determinants at 1.1 and 2.1 Å), GENIE is again far ahead of DMET+SQD at similar size, 6.2 against 29 kcal mol -1 and 22.5 against 94 kcal mol -1 at about 200 determinants, and without cap reaches 0.48 and 0.62 kcal mol -1 with 0.3 and 1.2 % of the space [Fig. 5 (b), Table 9 ]. Against classical selection in the MO basis at the same sizes it is behind, however: tied with CIPSI and ASCI at 200 determinants and 1.1 Å (6.25 vs. 6.14), 1.9 times behind at 2.1 Å (22.5 vs. 11.7), and 23 and 12 times behind uncapped (0.48 vs. 0.021 and 0.62 vs. 0.053 kcal mol -1 ). In the larger space, the 80-operator circuit reaches chemical accuracy but not the compact expansion that CIPSI finds. For H 14 , DMET truncates the system to 9–10 of 14 orbitals and the embedding is genuine (Table 1 , Fig. 6 ). Near equilibrium GENIE ties with CIPSI at 200 determinants, and with N ≈ 7 000 N\approx 7\,000 free-angle circuits reach the embedding FCI. At 1.5 Å it is 1.2 times behind CIPSI at 10 4 10^{4} determinants. At 2.0 Å and 80 operators it fails: 68–70 kcal mol -1 against 6–7 kcal mol -1 for CIPSI and ASCI at the same 10 4 10^{4} determinants, identically for both seeds and both angle schemes. At 1.5 and 2.0 Å every 80-operator run fills the cap of 10 4 10^{4} determinants (15.7 % of the space), so the limit is not the number of determinants but which ones the circuit reaches. Doubling the circuit to 160 operators recovers CIPSI quality [Fig. 6 (b)]: 7.92 kcal mol -1 against 7.00 for CIPSI; 320 operators add nothing (8.09 kcal mol -1 ). III.8 Scope and the LAS alternative This is an impurity-level study: every error above is measured against the exact solution of the same embedding Hamiltonian, which isolates the solver. The total DMET energy of a single impurity is not a whole-molecule energy; for H 10 it lies 77–386 kcal mol -1 above whole-molecule FCI, increasingly so on stretching, independently of the solver (App. H ). A whole-molecule comparison requires all fragments and an energy partitioning, which we leave to future work, as do the embedding errors that impurity-level benchmarks cannot see [ 24 , 19 ] . For spread states the router points to fragment methods. On H 10 , where whole-molecule FCI is available, LASSQD agrees with LASSCF to within 1 kcal mol -1 , but the error against FCI depends on the fragmentation: 38.5, 41.0 and 19.5 kcal mol -1 with H 2 -unit fragments at 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 Å, and 84.5, 32.5 and 9.5 kcal mol -1 with two halves (App. H ). For [Fe(H 2 O) 4 ] 2 bpym 4+ , where a DMET impurity would need about 40 qubits, LAS needs two ten-qubit fragments; our LASSCF lies 1.05 m E h E_{\mathrm{h}} below the published value [ 29 ] , and LASSQD warm-started from it reproduces it to 0.3 ​ μ ​ E h 0.3\,\mu E_{\mathrm{h}} for all four circuit/seed combinations (App. I ).
